known_final_diagnosis: This female infant demonstrates a case of Bartter syndrome type II with compound heterozygosity for two different pathogenic KCNJ1 gene variants who developed resolution of hyponatremia by 7 weeks of age while the classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis was not seen on follow up.

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: Premature female infant (33+6 weeks, 1450g) with antenatal polyhydramnios and possible duplex collecting system, presenting with poor responsiveness, dehydration, and 22% weight loss. Clinical presentation and family history of Bartter syndrome type II (KCNJ1 mutations) suggests early-onset salt-wasting disorder with electrolyte abnormalities and polyuria/polydipsia. Initial electrolyte derangements would be expected to show hyponatremia and hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis.

report.source_text: The patient required sodium chloride supplementation up to a maximum dose of 7.9 mmol/kg/day included in the total parenteral nutrition, started on day of life 7 to gradually achieve normal sodium levels. A trial of fludrocortisone therapy was recommended by endocrinology to definitively rule out CAH. The patient received two doses given on day 9 (0.03 mg/kg/dose) of life and was without clinical response. The patient’s electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks of life and supplementation was gradually weaned off by 7 weeks of life.

report.source_text: Results showed two pathogenic variants in the KCNJ1 gene [1]: a paternally inherited frameshift deletion, p.Glu334Glyfs*35 (c.996_999del, exon 5), predicted to result in premature protein termination and previously reported as causative for Bartter syndrome [6], and [2] a maternally inherited missense variant, p. Pro110Leu (c.329C > T, exon 5) (Fig. 2), previously reported to be pathogenic in compound heterozygosity with other pathogenic variants in KCNJ1 [8–10].

Early presentation shows mixed acid-base disturbance (respiratory acidosis with elevated HCO3- at 15h: pH 7.26, pCO2 59, HCO3- 28.3) combined with atypical electrolyte abnormalities: hyponatremia (121-137 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (5.5-8.0 mmol/L), and hypochloremia (86-100 mmol/L) in first 7 days. Urine electrolytes on day 7 show high sodium (118 mmol/L) consistent with renal salt-wasting. Treatment with sodium chloride supplementation (up to 7.9 mmol/kg/day) started day 7; fludrocortisone trial on day 9 without response. Electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks and supplementation weaned by 7 weeks. Genetic testing confirmed compound heterozygous KCNJ1 variants: paternally inherited frameshift deletion p.Glu334Glyfs*35 and maternally inherited missense variant p.Pro110Leu. This atypical presentation with hyperkalemia (rather than classic hypokalemia) and documented salt-wasting is consistent with KCNJ1-mediated Bartter syndrome type II.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Bartter syndrome type II with compound heterozygosity for two different pathogenic KCNJ1 gene variants
clinician.trajectory_summary: A female infant born at 33+6 weeks with very low birth weight (1450 g) and antenatal polyhydramnios presented on day 1 of life with poor responsiveness, dehydration, and 22% weight loss requiring non-invasive ventilation. Initial blood gas at 15 hours showed mixed acid-base disturbance (pH 7.26, pCO2 59 mmHg, HCO3- 28.3 mmol/L). Serum electrolytes over the first 7 days revealed an atypical pattern: hyponatremia (121-137 mmol/L), hyperkalemia (5.5-8.0 mmol/L), and hypochloremia (86-100 mmol/L)—distinct from classic Bartter syndrome which typically presents with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Urine electrolytes on day 7 documented renal salt-wasting with high urinary sodium (118 mmol/L), low potassium (7 mmol/L), and chloride (94 mmol/L), with osmolality of 369 mOsm/kg. Treatment initiated on day 7 with sodium chloride supplementation (maximum 7.9 mmol/kg/day); fludrocortisone trial on day 9 was ineffective. Electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks of life and supplementation was weaned by 7 weeks. Genetic testing confirmed compound heterozygous KCNJ1 variants: paternally inherited frameshift deletion p.Glu334Glyfs*35 (c.996_999del, exon 5) and maternally inherited missense variant p.Pro110Leu (c.329C > T, exon 5). Follow-up at 6 months showed sustained normal electrolytes (sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L) without development of the classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
